content_voiceover: This slide shows the mixing test, which helps you tell apart a factor deficiency from a factor inhibitor when a patient has a prolonged clotting time. You take the patient's plasma, which here has a PTT of eighty seconds, and mix it one to one with normal pooled plasma, which has a PTT of thirty five seconds. On the left side, if the problem is a simple factor deficiency, mixing in normal plasma supplies the missing factor, and the PTT corrects all the way down to thirty five seconds, matching normal. On the right side, if the patient has a factor inhibitor, such as an antibody neutralizing a clotting factor, adding normal plasma does not fully correct the PTT. After mixing and incubation it only comes down to sixty seconds, staying prolonged because the inhibitor is still actively neutralizing factor in the mixture. That failure to correct is the hallmark of an inhibitor, and it's a key concept tested repeatedly on hematology boards.
keypoints: Mix patient plasma one to one with normal pooled plasma
Correction to normal PTT suggests factor deficiency
Persistent prolongation suggests a factor inhibitor
Incubation helps unmask time-dependent inhibitors like factor eight inhibitor
keypoint_voiceover: To summarize, mixing patient plasma with normal plasma and checking whether the PTT corrects is the core of this test. Full correction points to a factor deficiency, since normal plasma restores what's missing. Persistent prolongation after mixing points to an inhibitor, because the antibody keeps neutralizing factor even in the mixed sample. Incubating the mix can also unmask inhibitors that need time to act.
